title: EPA Proposes Repeal of the Clean Power Plan
description_short: EPA announced a proposed repeal of the Clean Power Plan, reversing the Obama-era climate rule for power plants.
description_medium: On October 10, 2017, EPA proposed repealing the Clean Power Plan, the Obama administration’s rule for reducing carbon emissions from existing power plants. Administrator Scott Pruitt announced the change as the first step toward replacing the plan. The proposal began a rulemaking process; it did not itself erase the standards then in force.
description_long: The Environmental Protection Agency announced its proposal to repeal the Clean Power Plan on October 10, 2017. The plan, adopted under President Barack Obama, set a federal framework for reducing carbon pollution from existing power plants. EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt presented repeal as a shift away from the previous administration’s approach to climate regulation. Because this was a proposed rule, states, utilities, and the public could respond during the rulemaking before EPA finalized a replacement. The proposal did not immediately change the obligations that applied to power plants. It opened a broader dispute over how much authority the federal government should use to curb emissions from electricity generation and how that work should be divided between federal and state regulators. The administration later issued the Affordable Clean Energy rule as its replacement, but that later action was separate from the October announcement. The proposal marked the start of a major reversal in federal climate policy, while its practical effects depended on subsequent rules and court decisions.

preserved_fields.title: EPA Proposes Repeal of the Clean Power Plan
preserved_fields.description_short: EPA announced a proposed repeal of the Clean Power Plan, reversing the Obama-era climate rule for power plants.

title: Revokes Drone Strike Civilian Casualty Reporting Requirement

description_medium: On March 6, 2019, Donald Trump signed an executive order ending annual public reports on civilian deaths caused by U.S. strikes outside recognized war zones. The requirement had been introduced to make casualty information part of the government’s regular disclosures. The order changed what the public would routinely receive about those operations; it did not change strike authorization or targeting rules.
description_long: Donald Trump signed an executive order on March 6, 2019, revoking the requirement for annual reports on civilian deaths from U.S. strikes outside recognized war zones. The reporting rule had called for the government to publish a yearly accounting of civilian casualties in those operations. Ending it removed one regular source of public information about the human consequences of drone and other airstrikes. Lawmakers, journalists, and researchers had used such disclosures to compare government statements with reports from affected communities and independent monitors. The order concerned transparency; it did not itself authorize a new strike or amend the legal standards for selecting targets. Nor does the change alone show whether civilian casualties rose or fell. It narrowed the government’s routine public accounting at a time when the United States continued conducting counterterrorism operations abroad. The decision therefore made scrutiny of those operations more difficult, even as other reporting and oversight channels remained available.

title: Finalizes Affordable Clean Energy Rule
description_short: EPA finalized the Affordable Clean Energy rule, replacing the Clean Power Plan and weakening power plant emissions limits.
description_medium: On June 19, 2019, EPA finalized the Affordable Clean Energy rule, replacing the Clean Power Plan as the federal standard for emissions from existing power plants. The new rule took a narrower approach to reducing power-sector pollution. Its adoption completed the regulatory reversal that began with the 2017 repeal proposal.
description_long: The Environmental Protection Agency finalized the Affordable Clean Energy rule on June 19, 2019. It replaced the Clean Power Plan, the Obama-era framework for reducing carbon pollution from existing power plants. The Trump administration’s rule focused on changes at individual facilities rather than the broader system-wide approach of its predecessor. EPA described it as a different way to regulate emissions; environmental groups argued that it weakened federal limits and would allow higher pollution. The final rule gave states a new framework for setting performance standards, while leaving questions about the rule’s legal basis and expected emissions effects to later review. The change was a concrete step beyond the administration’s 2017 proposal to repeal the Clean Power Plan. It shifted federal climate policy away from the previous rule and changed what states and utilities would be asked to do. Subsequent court decisions affected the rule’s implementation, so the 2019 finalization should be understood as a policy action rather than the end of the legal dispute.

title: Terminates TPS for Sudan
description_short: The Federal Register announced termination of Temporary Protected Status for Sudan, starting a wind-down for Sudanese TPS holders.
description_medium: On October 11, 2017, the Federal Register published the decision to end Sudan’s Temporary Protected Status designation. The termination began a wind-down for eligible Sudanese beneficiaries, who had been allowed to live and work in the United States while conditions prevented safe return. Publication started a transition period; it did not mean every beneficiary was immediately deported.
description_long: The Department of Homeland Security’s decision to terminate Sudan’s Temporary Protected Status designation was published in the Federal Register on October 11, 2017. TPS had allowed eligible Sudanese nationals already in the United States to remain temporarily and obtain work authorization while the government judged that return was unsafe. Ending the designation began a transition period for people who had relied on that protection. The notice did not remove every beneficiary immediately: individual eligibility, deadlines, and any extensions determined what happened next. For affected families, the decision created uncertainty about legal status, employment, and the possibility of being required to leave the country. The change was part of the administration’s review of several TPS designations. It narrowed a humanitarian protection program that had shielded people from removal because of conditions in their home country. The published notice set out the government’s decision and transition process; later court actions and extensions would affect the timeline for Sudanese beneficiaries.

title: Pardons John Arthur Johnson, aka Jack Johnson
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to John Arthur Johnson, aka Jack Johnson as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On May 24, 2018, Donald Trump pardoned John Arthur “Jack” Johnson, the pioneering Black heavyweight boxing champion convicted under the Mann Act in 1913. Johnson had been targeted after crossing state lines with a white girlfriend. The pardon came nearly a century after his conviction and followed years of public advocacy for posthumous clemency.
description_long: Donald Trump granted a posthumous pardon to boxer John Arthur “Jack” Johnson on May 24, 2018. Johnson, the first Black heavyweight champion, had been convicted in 1913 under the Mann Act after traveling across state lines with a white woman who was his girlfriend. The prosecution took place amid racist hostility toward Johnson and his success in a sport dominated by white champions. He served time in prison and spent years abroad before returning to the United States. Johnson died in 1946. The pardon followed a long campaign by activists, lawmakers, and sports figures who argued that the conviction was racially motivated and unjust. Trump’s clemency order removed the federal conviction’s legal stigma, though it could not undo the harm Johnson suffered during his life. The action was included among the president’s clemency grants and drew renewed attention to how criminal law had been used against interracial relationships. The pardon recognized a historical injustice more than a century after the conviction.

description_long: Maryland and the District of Columbia filed suit against Donald Trump on June 12, 2017, alleging that his privately owned businesses received payments and advantages from foreign governments and from U.S. states. The complaint argued that those benefits violated the Constitution’s Foreign and Domestic Emoluments Clauses, which restrict certain payments to federal officeholders. The plaintiffs said Trump’s continued ownership of hotels and other businesses created conflicts while he served as president. It reflected wider concern about how constitutional limits apply when a president retains private commercial interests. title: FCC Repeals Net Neutrality Under Trump Appointees
description_short: The Trump-era FCC voted to repeal the 2015 net neutrality rules, rolling back federal protections for open internet access.
description_medium: On December 14, 2017, the Federal Communications Commission voted to repeal the 2015 net-neutrality rules. Those rules barred broadband providers from blocking, throttling, or favoring internet traffic. The repeal shifted federal oversight toward a lighter approach and renewed debate over whether providers should be able to influence what users can access or how online services reach customers.
description_long: The Federal Communications Commission voted on December 14, 2017, to repeal net-neutrality rules adopted in 2015. Those rules prohibited broadband providers from blocking lawful content, slowing selected services, or charging online platforms for preferential delivery. FCC Chairman Ajit Pai, appointed by Donald Trump, led the repeal effort. Supporters argued that removing the rules would reduce regulation and encourage investment; opponents warned that providers could gain more control over what customers see and which services compete effectively. The vote ended the Obama-era federal framework, although state laws and later litigation continued to shape the debate. The issue reaches beyond technical network management: broadband companies provide access to the internet while also deciding how their networks carry data. Repealing common protections changed the balance between federal oversight and provider discretion. The action did not prove that companies would immediately block or throttle services, but it removed rules designed to prevent those practices. The decision became a central dispute over open internet access and the reach of federal regulation.

title: Weakens Mercury and Air Toxics Standards Finding
description_short: EPA finalized a rule rescinding the "appropriate and necessary" finding underpinning mercury and air toxics standards for power plants.
description_medium: On May 22, 2020, EPA rescinded the “appropriate and necessary” finding that supported federal mercury and air-toxics standards for power plants. The finding formed part of the legal basis for limits on hazardous emissions. The change challenged the standards’ foundation, though it did not immediately switch off every pollution control already operating at power plants.
description_long: The Environmental Protection Agency finalized an action on May 22, 2020, rescinding the “appropriate and necessary” finding that underpinned the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for power plants. Those standards limit emissions of mercury and other hazardous pollutants linked to serious health risks. The finding was part of the agency’s legal rationale for regulating those emissions, so removing it called the rule’s foundation into question. EPA’s action did not mean that every pollution-control device at a power plant stopped operating that day; the standards and their implementation involved separate regulatory steps. The change nevertheless threatened the durability of protections that had required power plants to reduce toxic emissions. Public-health advocates argued that weaker controls could expose nearby communities to greater pollution, while industry groups challenged the costs and basis of the rule. The action focused on the agency’s justification for regulating, rather than a new measurement of emissions or health outcomes. Litigation and subsequent rulemaking would determine what protections remained in force.

title: House Impeaches Trump for Abuse of Power and Obstruction
description_short: The House of Representatives impeached Trump on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress related to Ukraine.
description_medium: The House impeached Donald Trump on December 18, 2019, approving articles charging abuse of power and obstruction of Congress over his dealings with Ukraine. One article concerned pressure on Ukraine to announce investigations that could benefit Trump politically; the other addressed the administration’s resistance to congressional oversight. The House vote sent the case to the Senate and did not itself remove Trump from office.
description_long: On December 18, 2019, the House of Representatives voted to impeach President Donald Trump on two charges arising from his dealings with Ukraine. The abuse-of-power article focused on Trump’s effort to have Ukraine announce investigations that could benefit him politically, including an inquiry into Joe Biden and his son. The obstruction article addressed the administration’s refusal to comply with congressional requests for documents and testimony. The House vote formally approved the articles and sent them to the Senate for trial. Impeachment is a constitutional accusation by the House, not a criminal conviction or automatic removal from office. The Senate considered the charges separately and ultimately acquitted Trump. The case centered on the limits of presidential authority in foreign policy and the extent to which Congress could investigate executive conduct. The vote made Trump the third U.S. president to be impeached. It also became part of a larger dispute over whether the president had used official power for personal political advantage.

description_long:

A district judge had halted most aboveground construction while allowing underground national-security work to continue under conditions. The appeals court issued an administrative stay to give itself time to consider the administration’s motion.

The stay was procedural and was not a decision on the merits. Reporting estimated the project at $400 million and described Trump as saying it would be privately financed. The legal dispute concerned presidential authority and historic preservation. The appeals court did not decide whether construction was lawful or who would ultimately prevail; it temporarily changed which work could proceed while the appeal was considered.
